title: Why Japan's Cricket Moment Signals the Game's Global Ambition
excerpt: Cricket's arrival in Japan — the Asian Games plus a historic first senior men's T20I against India on September 22 — is a deliberate bet on taking the game beyond its traditional markets, and the broadcast money is following.
body:
• Cricket arrives in Japan at an unprecedented moment: the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya plus a historic first senior men's T20I between India and Japan on September 22.
  • Japan Cricket's "City of Cricket" strategy builds the sport city by city — grounds, schools, community — with the Games serving as a catalyst in a region where cricket has no footing.
  • Broadcast deals are done: FanCode streams the Suzuki Cup in India, JioStar carries television rights, and ITW Universe holds exclusive global production and distribution rights.
  • For the sport's rulers, Japan is the test case for cricket's expansion beyond its traditional markets and toward its Olympic future.

A country that never played the game now hosts it

Cricket will be staged at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, with the women's competition running September 17 to 22 and the men's tournament September 24 to October 3. The matches will be played at Kōrogi Sports Park in Nisshin City — a region where organised cricket has, until now, had almost no presence.

That absence is precisely what makes Japan significant. Four days before the men's Asian Games tournament begins, India and Japan will meet in their first-ever senior-level men's T20I — the Suzuki Cup at the Sano International Cricket Ground in Tochigi Prefecture on September 22, with the first ball at 9:30 AM IST. The fixture marks 75 years of diplomatic relations between India and Japan and launches Sport 75, an initiative aimed at using sport to strengthen people-to-people exchanges between the two countries. India, the reigning T20 world champions under Shreyas Iyer, face a Japan side ranked 41st in the ICC T20I rankings.

Cricket diplomacy by design

BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia framed the fixture as deliberate policy rather than a friendly. "This is a significant moment for cricket, as it takes the Indian team to new territory and provides an opportunity to introduce the sport to a wider audience in Japan and East Asia," Saikia said in the BCCI's announcement, adding that the board believes "the growth of cricket must extend beyond its traditional territories, and as the world's largest cricket board, we recognise our responsibility to contribute to that growth."

In a post on X, Saikia credited the effort to the sport's top leadership: "Cricket's global journey is being shaped by moments that take the game beyond its traditional boundaries... It is also an opportunity to recognise the vision and groundwork laid by Shri Jay Shah during his tenure as BCCI Secretary, and now as ICC Chairman, in placing the global growth of cricket firmly at the heart of the sport's future — from expanding cricket into new territories to building a stronger pathway towards the Olympic movement."

Japan's ground-up playbook

Japan Cricket Association CEO Naoki Miyaji has spent years preparing the ground, literally, for this moment. The association's strategy is not to spread the sport thin across the country but to build it city by city. "We've been doing this 'City of Cricket' strategy, where we identify a city and then we try to build a cricket ecosystem in that city," Miyaji told myKhel. "We try to get a ground, we try to get into schools, we try to get the local community involved, and then we build from there."

He was candid about how slow the work is. "The first school is so hard. Getting the first ground is so hard. Moving from city to city, it's not easy. But once you have that foothold, once you have that first group of children playing and that first facility, then you can start to build something that is sustainable." For Aichi-Nagoya, the Asian Games are the shortcut: "The challenge has been that we're hosting one of the biggest sports events in the world in a place where the sport has no footing," Miyaji said. Nisshin City's Games exposure, he believes, can provide the catalyst to establish a permanent cricketing presence in the region.

"On the social impact, the economic impact, the partner impact, the market impact, and the media impact, having that full-strength side means the world to us."

— Naoki Miyaji, CEO, Japan Cricket Association

"To be able to invite the reigning World Champions to the home of cricket in Japan is a landmark moment for our association," Miyaji said of the India visit, urging Japanese fans and those simply curious about the sport to attend and support the home side.

The media money follows

The commercial side of the moment has been resolved. FanCode bagged the streaming rights for the September 22 match in the India region, while JioStar secured television broadcast rights in India; ITW Universe holds the exclusive global sports production, broadcast distribution and commercial marketing rights for the fixture. Reporting indicates YouTube and Netflix may enter the fray for the international digital rights — a sign that the fixture's value comes as much from what it represents as from who plays in it. As the organisers' media statement put it, the match presents "an unprecedented opportunity to take Indian cricket into a new market and build long-term visibility in Japan."

Earlier reports had flagged broadcaster uncertainty around the one-off fixture — a standalone match 400 kilometres from the Asian Games hub, at a ground with a standard capacity of just 500, carries real production cost and logistics. That the rights picture closed with major players involved says something about how seriously the market now treats cricket's expansion frontier.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora, Japan is the new front row. The Indian community in Japan — and cricket fans across East Asia — get a rare live sighting of the world champions, while the diaspora's global streaming audience is the commercial engine that makes a fixture like this worth broadcasting in the first place.

What's Next

The women's Asian Games cricket competition is already underway, with the Suzuki Cup T20I on September 22 serving as India's warm-up before the men's Asian Games tournament begins on September 24. The real measure of Japan's moment, though, comes after October 3: whether Nisshin City still has cricket when the Games leave.
